questions.title: Who you tell
questions.question: You think a cyber incident may have happened. Under your IRP, who must you tell?

options.label: The CSIRT, promptly
Your manager, at your next check-in
The IT provider only
No one, until you are sure it is an incident

questions.explanation: Your IRP requires every Supervised Person to promptly notify the CSIRT listed in Appendix D. The FAQ in Appendix E says the same: reach out to the CSIRT promptly.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.5 Incident Handling Standard; Appendix E, question 2
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3): response program reasonably designed to detect, respond to and recover from unauthorized access to or use of customer information
questions.tie_in: The response program starts only when the CSIRT knows. Prompt internal reporting is how detection reaches the people who respond.

questions.title: Reporting your own mistake
questions.question: You clicked a link in an email and now think it was a phishing attempt. What does your IRP say about reporting it?

options.label: Reporting is mandatory. An honest mistake is excusable, staying silent is not.
Report it only if you are sure it caused harm, so the CSIRT is not distracted
Try to fix it yourself first, and report it only if the problem continues
Reporting is optional when no client data was stored on your computer

questions.explanation: Your IRP says reporting a potential incident is mandatory, even if you caused it by accident. Human error is excusable. Not reporting out of fear or apathy is not. Appendix E adds: you will not get in trouble for reporting.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.3.2 Supervised Persons; Appendix E, question 5
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3): response program reasonably designed to detect unauthorized access to or use of customer information
questions.tie_in: A firm cannot detect what its people hide. Blame-free reporting is how the program finds incidents early enough to contain them and notify on time.

questions.title: When both leads are out
questions.question: During an incident, neither the {{csirtLead}} nor the {{secondaryLead}} can be reached. Under your IRP, who leads the response?

options.label: Any CSIRT member may take the lead, and that choice is recorded in the incident log
The response waits until one of the two leads can be reached and approves it
AdvisorDefense takes the lead and makes every decision on the firm's behalf
The first employee who noticed the incident leads until a lead is reachable

questions.explanation: Appendix D says the {{secondaryLead}} steps in when the {{csirtLead}} is unavailable. If both are unavailable, any CSIRT member may assume the lead, and the selection is documented in the incident log.
questions.irp_ref: Appendix D CSIRT Roles and Responsibilities
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3): response program reasonably designed to detect, respond to and recover from unauthorized access
questions.tie_in: A clear line of succession means the response program still runs when key people are away.

questions.title: AdvisorDefense's role
questions.question: What role does AdvisorDefense have under your IRP?

options.label: A named member of the CSIRT that helps respond to incidents
An outside vendor the firm calls only after the incident is closed
The firm's breach counsel, engaged through the insurance carrier
The party that decides on the firm's behalf whether clients are notified

questions.explanation: Appendix D lists AdvisorDefense as a CSIRT member, with its support phone and email. AdvisorDefense also reviews suspicious emails and supports containment (Appendix A). The firm still owns its decisions, including whether to notify clients.
questions.irp_ref: Appendix D CSIRT Roles and Responsibilities; Appendix C Key Contact List
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3): response program reasonably designed to detect, respond to and recover from unauthorized access
questions.tie_in: Naming outside expertise inside the team shows the program has the resources to detect, contain and recover.

questions.title: Annual IRP review
questions.question: Has the firm reviewed and updated its IRP, including the CSIRT names and contacts in Appendix D, in the last 12 months?

options.label: Yes, and the revision history shows it
Reviewed, but changes were not made or not recorded
No or not sure

questions.help: People change roles and phone numbers change. The SEC says firms generally should review and update their response procedures periodically so they stay reasonably designed.
questions.exam_finding: The firm could not show that it periodically reviews and updates its incident response program, including the personnel responsible for responding to incidents.
questions.irp_ref: Document Information and Revision History; Appendix D
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3); Release No. 34-100155, section II.A: covered institutions generally should consider reviewing and updating response procedures periodically (guidance, not a rule requirement)
questions.tie_in: A plan with old names and numbers is not reasonably designed. The annual review keeps the IRP able to do what Reg S-P requires.

questions.title: Practice run
questions.question: Has the CSIRT practiced the IRP with a tabletop exercise in the last 12 months?

options.label: Yes, and we updated the IRP afterward
Yes, but over 12 months ago, or no updates followed
No or not sure

questions.help: A tabletop is a guided walk-through of a simulated incident. Reg S-P does not require one, but it is the usual way to show the plan works and to find gaps before a real incident does.
questions.exam_finding: The firm could not show that it tests or periodically reviews its incident response procedures, for example through a tabletop exercise followed by documented plan updates.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.3.2 Supervised Persons; Section 3.10 Post-Incident Assessment and Enhancement
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3); Release No. 34-100155, section II.A: periodic review and update of response procedures (guidance, not a rule requirement)
questions.tie_in: Practice turns the written IRP into a program the firm can actually run, which is what Reg S-P expects.

questions.title: What counts as an incident
questions.question: Which of these is an incident you must report under your IRP?

options.label: You emailed a client's statement to the wrong person
A coworker asks you to resend a meeting invite
Your laptop restarts to install scheduled updates
A client calls to update their mailing address on file

questions.explanation: Appendix E lists sending a sensitive email to the wrong recipient as an incident, along with malware, a lost or stolen device and any breach of personal information. If you are ever in doubt, treat it as an incident and report it.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.1 Definition of an Incident; Appendix E, question 1
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3): response program reasonably designed to detect unauthorized access to or use of customer information
questions.tie_in: Detection starts with people recognizing an incident. A misdirected email can be unauthorized access to client information.

questions.title: How fast to report
questions.question: How quickly should you report a possible incident to the CSIRT?

options.label: As soon as you become aware of it
By the end of the business day
Within 72 hours of noticing it
Once you have confirmed it is real

questions.explanation: Appendix E says to report as soon as you become aware. Fast reporting matters because notification and regulatory deadlines can start at the moment of discovery.
questions.irp_ref: Appendix E, question 3; Section 2.5 Incident Handling Standard
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(4)(iii): client notice due as soon as practicable, no later than 30 days after becoming aware of unauthorized access
questions.tie_in: The 30-day client notice clock runs from when the firm becomes aware. Every day of delayed internal reporting uses up that time.

questions.title: After entering your password
questions.question: You entered your password on a login page you now think was fake. Under your IRP, what should you do?

options.label: Report it right away, then change your password from a different, trusted device
Change your password on the same device, and report it only if something odd happens
Delete the email right away so no one else at the firm can click the same link
Run your own antivirus scan first, and report it only if the scan finds something

questions.explanation: Appendix E says: report it immediately, change your password from a different, trusted device, keep the email for the CSIRT, and watch for unexpected logins, MFA prompts or payment requests. Disconnect from the network only if instructed.
questions.irp_ref: Appendix E, question 5
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3): response program reasonably designed to detect and respond to unauthorized access to or use of customer information
questions.tie_in: Stolen credentials are a common path to client information. Fast reporting and a clean password reset help the firm detect and contain the access.

questions.title: Sending a suspicious email
questions.question: How should you send a suspicious email to the CSIRT?

options.label: Forward it as an attachment so the full headers can be inspected
Forward it inline like a normal email so the CSIRT can read it quickly
Take a screenshot for the CSIRT, then delete the original message
Reply to the sender first and ask whether the message is genuine

questions.explanation: Appendix E says to forward a suspicious email to the CSIRT as an attachment, not inline, so the headers can be inspected. Do not delete it, reply to it, click its links or open its attachments.
questions.irp_ref: Appendix E, questions 4 and 6; Appendix A, Phishing
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3)(i): assess the nature and scope of an incident
questions.tie_in: The original message is evidence. Keeping it intact lets the CSIRT assess what happened and who else received it.

questions.title: Level 1 response time
questions.question: Under your IRP, how quickly must the CSIRT begin responding to a Level 1 incident, and how often must it send status updates?

options.label: Within {{level1Response}}, with status updates {{level1Updates}}
Within 4 hours, with status updates every 2 hours
Within 24 hours, with daily status updates
Within 48 hours, with daily status updates

questions.explanation: Level 1 incidents affect critical systems or information and could impact revenue or clients, such as a breach of sensitive data or an active attacker. The IRP sets an initial response within {{level1Response}} and status updates {{level1Updates}}.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.4 Incident Criticality
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3)(i) and (ii): assess, contain and control an incident involving unauthorized access
questions.tie_in: Defined response times show the program is reasonably designed to act fast enough to contain an incident.

questions.title: Sensitive customer information
questions.question: Which of these is sensitive customer information under your IRP?

options.label: A client's account number together with their date of birth
A client's name together with the city and state they live in
The firm's public Form ADV brochure, as posted on the SEC website
A list of the firm's office phone numbers and general email address

questions.explanation: Your IRP defines sensitive customer information to include an account number or name combined with information that could be used to get into the account, such as a date of birth, an access code or a security question answer. A Social Security number on its own also counts.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.2 Sensitive Customer Information Classification and Definitions
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(d)(9): definition and examples of sensitive customer information
questions.tie_in: Notice duties under Reg S-P turn on sensitive customer information. Knowing it on sight is how people know an incident is serious.

questions.title: Assessing scope
questions.question: Under your IRP, what does the CSIRT's scope assessment cover?

options.label: The systems and data involved, how the data is classified, and the effect on operations
The cost of restoring the affected systems and whether the insurance policy will cover it
Whether law enforcement should be called, and which agency should receive the report
Which employee caused the incident, and what discipline the firm should consider for them

questions.explanation: Section 3.3 says the CSIRT uses logs and other available information to assess which systems and data might be involved, notes how the information is classified, and decides whether operations are affected. If they are, the Business Continuity Plan is invoked as needed.
questions.irp_ref: Section 3.3 Assessment of Potential Scope
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3)(i): assess the nature and scope of an incident and identify the systems and types of customer information involved
questions.tie_in: The scope assessment is the step Reg S-P names first. It decides who may need notice and what must be contained.

questions.title: Where client data lives
questions.question: If one of the firm's systems were breached, could the CSIRT tell which clients' sensitive information was in it?

options.label: Yes, we know what client information each system holds
For some systems, not all
No or not sure

questions.help: If the firm cannot tell whose information was accessed, Reg S-P generally requires notice to every individual whose sensitive information was in the affected system.
questions.exam_finding: The firm has not identified which customer information systems hold sensitive customer information, which limits its ability to assess the scope of an incident and identify the individuals who must be notified.
questions.irp_ref: Section 3.3 Assessment of Potential Scope; Section 2.2
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3)(i) identify the systems and information involved; 248.30(a)(4)(ii) notice to all individuals in an affected system when specific individuals cannot be identified
questions.tie_in: A current data map is what makes the IRP's scope assessment possible, and it limits notice to the clients actually affected.

questions.title: Handling an affected computer
questions.question: Your computer shows a ransom message. Under your IRP, what should you do with it?

options.label: Leave it on, and disconnect it from the network only if the CSIRT tells you to
Turn it off right away and unplug it, so the ransomware cannot spread any further
Restart it to see whether the message clears, then report it if it comes back
Take it to a local repair shop so they can remove the ransomware the same day

questions.explanation: Appendix E says not to power off, restart or reimage an affected device, and to disconnect it from the network only if the CSIRT instructs. Powering off can destroy evidence the CSIRT needs. Report it right away.
questions.irp_ref: Appendix E, question 4; Section 3.2 Protection of Forensic Data
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3)(ii): take appropriate steps to contain and control the incident
questions.tie_in: Containment must not destroy the evidence the firm needs to assess scope and decide on client notice.

questions.title: A demand for payment
questions.question: An email demands payment to stop the release of firm data. What should you do?

options.label: Do not pay or reply. Report it to the CSIRT.
Pay it if the amount is small, to protect clients
Reply to negotiate a lower amount, then report it
Forward it to clients so they are warned

questions.explanation: Appendix E says never to pay any money, ransom or invoice tied to an incident. Appendix A says any payment decision goes through outside counsel, the insurance carrier and a specialist firm, with mandatory sanctions screening.
questions.irp_ref: Appendix E, question 4; Appendix A, Ransomware
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3)(ii): take appropriate steps to contain and control the incident
questions.tie_in: Containment decisions are made by the CSIRT with counsel and the carrier. A payment by one person can break the law and the insurance terms.

questions.title: A call from a reporter
questions.question: A reporter calls you asking about a rumored breach at the firm. What should you say?

options.label: That you are not in a position to comment, and suggest they contact the CSIRT
Confirm only the facts you know for certain, so the story is accurate
Say firmly that nothing happened, so the rumor does not spread further
Tell them which clients were affected, so those clients hear it quickly

questions.explanation: Appendix E says not to respond to the media. For phone requests, say you are not in a position to comment and suggest they reach out to the CSIRT. Forward written requests to the CSIRT.
questions.irp_ref: Appendix E, question 8
questions.regsp_ref: none: media handling is an IRP control. Reg S-P governs the written notice to affected individuals in 248.30(a)(4), not press statements.
questions.tie_in: Uncoordinated statements can contradict the written client notice Reg S-P requires and expose client information.

questions.title: Calling law enforcement
questions.question: When may you contact law enforcement yourself about an incident?

options.label: Only if the CSIRT directs you to, or if someone is in personal danger
Any time you believe a crime may have happened, without waiting for anyone
Never, under any circumstances, even if someone is in personal danger
Only after the firm has finished notifying all affected clients

questions.explanation: Appendix E says not to contact law enforcement, media or others unless the CSIRT directs you to. The exception is personal danger or a crime against a person, such as a robbery or assault. Then call law enforcement promptly. Section 3.5 says law enforcement is involved only with the CSIRT's knowledge and approval.
questions.irp_ref: Appendix E, questions 2 and 7; Section 3.5 Escalation of the Incident
questions.regsp_ref: none: contacting law enforcement is an IRP control. Note that only a written determination by the U.S. Attorney General can delay Reg S-P client notice (248.30(a)(4)(iii)).
questions.tie_in: The CSIRT coordinates outside contacts so the investigation, the evidence and the notice timeline stay under control.

questions.title: Money movement
questions.question: An incident involves a compromised email account. Which containment step does your IRP call for on money movement?

options.label: Halt transfers and verify any wire or banking change through a separate, known channel
Process pending wires quickly, before the attacker has a chance to change the instructions
Approve transfers only after confirming by reply in the same email thread as the request
Leave transfers to the custodian to handle, without mentioning the incident to them

questions.explanation: Section 3.4 says to consider temporarily halting fund transfers and financial transactions. The Appendix A playbooks say to stop all money movement and verify any wire, ACH or banking detail change out of band before processing.
questions.irp_ref: Section 3.4 Containment of the Incident; Appendix A
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3)(ii): take appropriate steps to contain and control the incident to prevent further unauthorized access or use
questions.tie_in: Stopping money movement is the containment step that most directly prevents client harm while the firm assesses scope.

questions.title: Protecting evidence
questions.question: Which step follows your IRP for protecting forensic data during an incident?

options.label: Stop logs from being overwritten, and take and protect snapshots of affected virtual machines
Reimage the affected machines first to stop the attack, then collect whatever logs remain
Delete older logs to free up storage space so the investigation can run faster
Block the attacker by launching a counterattack on the server they are using

questions.explanation: Section 3.2 says to configure systems so evidence is not overwritten, change passwords on systems that hold forensic data, add storage if needed, keep disconnected systems intact and protect virtual machine snapshots. Section 3.4 prohibits any retaliation against the attacker.
questions.irp_ref: Section 3.2 Protection of Forensic Data; Section 3.4 Containment of the Incident
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3)(i) and (ii): assess scope, and contain and control the incident
questions.tie_in: Preserved logs are how the firm proves what was and was not accessed. That record supports the notice decision Reg S-P requires.

questions.title: Insurance, counsel and forensics
questions.question: In a likely data breach, what order does your IRP set for the insurance carrier, counsel and a forensic firm?

options.label: Call the carrier first, get breach counsel through the carrier, then forensics through counsel
Hire a forensic firm directly to save time, then tell the carrier when the invoice arrives
Finish notifying clients first, then file the insurance claim and engage counsel if needed
Have the IT provider investigate on its own and skip counsel to keep costs down

questions.explanation: Section 3.1 says {{carrier}} must be notified promptly and third parties engaged according to the policy. Appendix C says breach counsel is engaged through the carrier's claims hotline. Section 3.6 says forensic firms should be engaged through outside counsel.
questions.irp_ref: Section 3.1 Cybersecurity Insurance; Section 3.6 Involvement of Counsel; Appendix C
questions.regsp_ref: none: insurance and legal privilege are not Reg S-P requirements. They protect coverage and the investigation record.
questions.tie_in: Late carrier notice can put coverage at risk. Work done through counsel can help protect privilege while the firm makes its Reg S-P notice decision.

questions.title: After-action review
questions.question: Under your IRP, when must an after-action review happen?

options.label: For every incident, promptly after the incident is closed
Only for Level 1 incidents, within 30 days after they are closed
Only when clients were notified, after the notices have gone out
Once a year, combined with the annual review of the IRP

questions.explanation: Section 3.10 says an after-action analysis is performed for all incidents, with meetings held promptly after the incident closes. The goal is to document what happened, capture lessons learned and identify controls that reduce the risk of a repeat.
questions.irp_ref: Section 3.10 Post-Incident Assessment and Enhancement
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3): recover from unauthorized access; Release No. 34-100155, section II.A: review and update procedures periodically (guidance)
questions.tie_in: Lessons from each incident keep the program reasonably designed over time.

questions.title: Lessons learned
questions.question: After incidents and exercises, does the firm document lessons learned and update the IRP?

options.label: Yes, with a dated record of what changed
We discuss lessons, but do not document them or update the IRP
No or not sure

questions.help: An examiner may ask what the firm changed after its last incident or exercise. A dated after-action record answers that.
questions.exam_finding: The firm did not document post-incident reviews or show that lessons learned were used to update its incident response procedures.
questions.irp_ref: Section 3.10 Post-Incident Assessment and Enhancement; Revision History
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3); 17 CFR 275.204-2(a)(25)(ii) documentation of the response to, and recovery from, unauthorized access
questions.tie_in: Documented recovery and lessons learned are both evidence of the program and part of the record advisers must keep.

questions.title: Client notice deadline
questions.question: Under your IRP and Reg S-P, when must affected clients be notified?

options.label: As soon as practicable, and no later than 30 days after becoming aware of unauthorized access
Within 72 hours of discovering the incident, the same window that applies to vendors
Within 30 days after the investigation is finished and the scope is confirmed
Within 60 days, once breach counsel has reviewed and approved the notice wording

questions.explanation: Section 2.6 of your IRP matches the rule: notice is due as soon as practicable, but not later than 30 days, after the firm becomes aware that unauthorized access to or use of customer information has occurred or is reasonably likely to have occurred. The clock does not wait for the investigation to finish.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.6 Legal and Regulatory Notification Standard
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(4)(iii): timing of notice
questions.tie_in: This is the Reg S-P deadline itself. The IRP's reporting, scoping and containment steps exist so the firm can meet it.

questions.title: Deciding not to notify
questions.question: When may the firm decide that client notice is not required after unauthorized access?

options.label: Only if a reasonable investigation finds harm is not reasonably likely, and the basis is documented
Whenever no client has reported any harm or suspicious activity to the firm so far
Whenever the incident happened at a vendor's system rather than at the firm itself
Whenever fewer than 500 clients are affected and the data was only viewed, not copied

questions.explanation: Section 2.6 says notice is not required only if the firm determines the information has not been, and is not reasonably likely to be, used in a manner that would result in substantial harm or inconvenience. Section 3.7 requires a written record of that determination and the reasoning behind it.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.6 Legal and Regulatory Notification Standard; Section 3.7 Investigation of the Incident
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3)(iii) and (a)(4)(i): no-notice determination after a reasonable investigation; 17 CFR 275.204-2(a)(25)(iii): record of the basis
questions.tie_in: The rule presumes notice. The IRP's investigation and written reasoning are what let the firm defend a decision not to notify.

questions.title: Delaying notice
questions.question: Who can authorize a delay in Reg S-P client notice past the 30-day deadline?

options.label: The U.S. Attorney General, by a written determination sent to the SEC
The firm's breach counsel, if the investigation needs more time
The local police department investigating the incident, by request
The firm's cyber insurance carrier, under the terms of the policy

questions.explanation: Reg S-P allows a delay only if the U.S. Attorney General determines that notice poses a substantial risk to national security or public safety and tells the SEC in writing. Section 4 of your IRP requires keeping any written documentation from the Attorney General about a delay.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.6 Legal and Regulatory Notification Standard; Section 4 Maintenance of Books and Records
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(4)(iii): Attorney General delay
questions.tie_in: Counsel, police and carriers cannot stop the clock. Knowing this keeps the firm from missing the deadline on someone's informal request.

questions.title: Notice process and owner
questions.question: Does the firm have a written process, with a named role responsible, for notifying affected clients within the Reg S-P deadline?

options.label: Yes, it is written and a role owns it
We know the deadline but have no written process or owner
No or not sure

questions.help: The 30 days start when the firm becomes aware of unauthorized access, not when the investigation ends. Someone needs to own the clock from day one.
questions.exam_finding: The firm's written procedures do not define when the firm becomes aware of an incident or assign responsibility for notifying affected individuals as soon as practicable, and no later than 30 days after becoming aware of unauthorized access to or use of customer information.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.6 Legal and Regulatory Notification Standard; Section 3.9.3 Responding to Privacy Breaches
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(3)(iii) and (a)(4): customer notification procedures
questions.tie_in: The IRP is where the firm's notification procedures live. A named owner turns the rule's deadline into a task someone tracks.

questions.title: Notice ready to send
questions.question: Has the firm checked its client breach notice template (Appendix F) against the content Reg S-P requires?

options.label: Yes, it was checked against the rule and is ready to use
We have the template but have not checked it against the rule
No or not sure

questions.help: The rule lists what a notice must say, including what happened, what information was involved, how to reach the firm, and how clients can protect themselves. Drafting it during an incident uses up the 30 days.
questions.exam_finding: The firm has not prepared a customer notification template containing the elements Regulation S-P requires, including a description of the incident and the information involved, contact information, and steps affected individuals can take to protect themselves.
questions.irp_ref: Appendix F Data Subject Breach Notification
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(4)(iv)(A) to (H): notice contents
questions.tie_in: A checked template is how the IRP makes the notice content Reg S-P requires ready before it is needed.

questions.title: Vendor breach notice
questions.question: Under Reg S-P, how quickly must a service provider notify the firm of a breach affecting a system that holds the firm's client information?

options.label: As soon as possible, and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it
Within 30 days, the same deadline that applies to notifying clients
Within 7 business days, once the provider has confirmed the breach
Only once the provider decides that the firm's clients were harmed

questions.explanation: The firm's oversight must be reasonably designed to ensure providers notify the firm as soon as possible, but no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a breach resulting in unauthorized access to a customer information system they maintain. Section 2.7 of your IRP sets the same 72-hour window.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.7 Third-Party Vendor Oversight
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(5)(i)(B): service provider notice to the firm
questions.tie_in: The firm's own 30-day clock can start when it hears from the vendor. The 72-hour limit keeps the vendor from using up that time.

questions.title: When a vendor is breached
questions.question: A vendor tells the firm it had a breach that may include client information. What happens next?

options.label: The CSIRT starts the firm's incident response, and the firm stays responsible for client notice
The firm waits for the vendor's final forensic report before it takes any action itself
Nothing more is needed, because the vendor is required to notify the firm's clients directly
The firm forwards the vendor's notice to all of its clients on the same day it arrives

questions.explanation: Section 2.5 says the CSIRT must be notified when the firm learns of a breach at a third party. Reg S-P requires the firm to start its incident response program when it receives the vendor's notice. A vendor may send notices for the firm under a written agreement, but the firm stays responsible for making sure they go out.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.5 Incident Handling Standard; Appendix A, Data Breach at Third-Party Vendor
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(5)(i)(B) initiate the response program on receipt; 248.30(a)(5)(ii) and (iii) the firm keeps the notice obligation
questions.tie_in: Outsourcing a system does not outsource the Reg S-P duty. The IRP treats a vendor breach as the firm's own incident.

questions.title: Vendor due diligence
questions.question: For each vendor that can access client information, has the firm reviewed and documented its security practices, and does it check them again over time?

options.label: Yes, for all of them
Some vendors, or only at onboarding
No or not sure

questions.help: Reg S-P requires oversight of vendors through due diligence and monitoring. Reports such as a SOC 2 can help, but the review should fit the vendor and what it can access.
questions.exam_finding: The firm has not documented due diligence and ongoing monitoring of service providers that receive, maintain, process or have access to customer information.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.7 Third-Party Vendor Oversight
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(5)(i): oversight, including through due diligence and monitoring; 248.30(d)(10) service provider definition
questions.tie_in: Section 2.7 is where the IRP commits to vendor review. Documented diligence is the evidence that it happens.

questions.title: 72-hour vendor commitments
questions.question: Can the firm show that its vendors with access to client information will notify it of a breach no later than 72 hours after becoming aware?

options.label: Yes, in writing, for all of them
Some vendors, or not in writing
No or not sure

questions.help: Reg S-P does not require a contract, but the firm must be able to show its oversight is reasonably designed to get notice within 72 hours. A contract clause, questionnaire answer or attestation are common ways to show it.
questions.exam_finding: The firm's service provider oversight does not ensure that service providers notify the firm as soon as possible, and no later than 72 hours, after becoming aware of a breach resulting in unauthorized access to a customer information system they maintain.
questions.irp_ref: Section 2.7 Third-Party Vendor Oversight
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 248.30(a)(5)(i)(B): 72-hour service provider notice
questions.tie_in: The IRP says the firm will consider questionnaires and attestations for this. Having them on file shows the oversight works.

questions.title: Records of a notice decision
questions.question: Which records must the firm keep about a decision on whether to notify clients?

options.label: The basis for the decision, any Attorney General delay record, and a copy of any notice sent
Only copies of the notice letters that were mailed, since those show the firm acted
Only the forensic firm's final report and invoice, which the carrier will require
Nothing, if the firm decided notice was not required, since no notice was sent

questions.explanation: Section 4 of your IRP lists written documentation of any investigation and determination on whether notice is required, including the basis for the determination, any written documentation from the U.S. Attorney General about a delay, and a copy of any notice sent.
questions.irp_ref: Section 4 Maintenance of Books and Records
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 275.204-2(a)(25)(iii): records of notification determinations
questions.tie_in: These records are how an examiner tests the firm's notice decisions. The IRP's recordkeeping section is how the firm keeps them.

questions.title: The incident log
questions.question: Under your IRP, where must the incident log be kept?

options.label: In the firm's compliance files
Only in the IT provider's ticketing system
In an email thread among the CSIRT
Nowhere, for Level 3 incidents

questions.explanation: The introduction to Section 3 and Appendix B say an incident log must be maintained in the firm's compliance files. The CSIRT Lead is responsible for documenting the incident (Appendix D).
questions.irp_ref: Section 3 introduction; Appendix B Incident Log; Appendix D
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 275.204-2(a)(25)(ii): documentation of detected unauthorized access and the response and recovery
questions.tie_in: The incident log is the core record an examiner asks for. Keeping it in compliance files means the firm controls it, not a vendor.

questions.title: Records ready for an exam
questions.question: If the SEC asked for the firm's Reg S-P policies, incident records and vendor oversight files, could the firm produce them within a few days?

options.label: Yes, everything is organized and ready
Some of it, but there would be gaps
No, we would be starting from scratch

questions.help: Advisers must keep the Reg S-P policies, incident documentation, notice determinations, vendor oversight policies and agreements, and disposal policies as books and records.
questions.exam_finding: The firm could not promptly produce written documentation of its incident response program, notification determinations, service provider oversight and procedures for disposal of customer information.
questions.irp_ref: Section 4 Maintenance of Books and Records
questions.regsp_ref: 17 CFR 275.204-2(a)(25)(i) to (vi): records investment advisers must make and keep
questions.tie_in: The IRP's recordkeeping section is the firm's index to the evidence Reg S-P asks for.
